title: 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC tanıtıldı: Shelby serisinin yeni halefi
summary: Ford, Shelby GT500 modelinin yerini alacak 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC'yi tanıttı. Süper şarjlı 5.2 litrelik V-8 motora sahip araç, 795 beygir güç üretiyor.
body:
Ford, Mustang ailesinin yeni performans zirvesi olan 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC modelini görücüye çıkardı. Car and Driver ve The Drive'ın aktardığına göre, Shelby adını geride bırakan süper şarjlı bu yeni otomobil, gücünü 5.2 litrelik çift eksantrik millidir 32 valfli V-8 motordan alıyor. S650 platformu üzerinde yükselen ve doğrudan eski GT500 modelinin yerini alan araç, 795 beygir güç ve 660 libre-fit tork sunuyor.

## Performans ve donanım paketleri

Araç gücünü arka tekerleklere Tremec marka yedi vitesli çift kavramalı otomatik şanzımanla aktarıyor. Standart versiyonun yanı sıra daha sert süspansiyona, Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R lastiklere ve karbon fiber jantlara sahip olan Track Pack paketi de sunuluyor. Bu paket, arka koltukların çıkarılması ve hafif parçalar sayesinde aracın ağırlığını 150 libre (yaklaşık 68 kilogram) azaltıyor. Sonoma Raceway ve Napa Valley'de gerçekleştirilen ilk sürüş testlerinde, adaptif MagneRide süspansiyonların bozuk zeminlerde bile yüksek denge sağladığı, karbon seramik frenlerin ise aracı güvenle durdurduğu belirtildi.

## Fiyat ve satış seçenekleri

Car and Driver'ın paylaştığı bilgilere göre, 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC modelinin standart versiyonu 108.085 dolardan başlayan fiyatlarla satışa çıkıyor. Track Pack donanımına sahip model 144.585 dolar etiket taşıyorken, en üst seviyedeki Special Edition versiyonu ise 175.565 dolarlık fiyat etiketine sahip.

**Neden önemli?** Shelby isminden vazgeçilerek Ford Performance ekibi tarafından geliştirilen Dark Horse SC, markanın pist odaklı mühendislik birikimini ve GTD modelinden alınan güncel teknolojileri daha erişilebilir bir performans coupe gövdesinde birleştiriyor.

source_texts.title: 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC Gallops at a Faster Pace
source_texts.summary: This next-level Mustang steps into the spot previously occupied by the Shelby GT500 in the stable.
source_texts.text:
Porsche perfected the concept of producing a hierarchy of variants of the same car, with increasing levels of performance, greater scarcity, and, of course, higher prices. The people in Chevrolet’s Corvette group have learned this lesson well, and the latest to adopt this strategy is Ford with the Mustang, as evidenced by the new Dark Horse SC, which sits just below the pinnacle of the Mustang roadgoing stable that is the GTD.
SC stands for supercharged, and this car is essentially the successor to the Shelby GT500, but on the current S650 Mustang platform. The reason it’s not called a Shelby is due to the latest shift in Ford Performance’s marketing musical chairs that goes back to the alphabet soup of SVO, SVT, SVE that we’ve seen over the years.
This time the change comes down to the company’s emphasis on Ford—or really Mustang—Racing (which is Ford Performance’s new name). Among the racing Mustangs already extant, you’ll find the Dark Horse R, the Mustang GT4, and the Mustang GT3. Moreover, these racing Mustangs and the various street cars are all developed by the same Ford Racing engineering team. And since there are no racing Shelbys, the latest model is divorced from that famous name and called a Dark Horse to keep it in the family.
Under the hood, you’ll find the double-overhead-camshaft 32-valve 5.2-liter V-8 that’s much like the one that motivated the GT500, the current F-150 Raptor R, and the Mustang GTD. It uses the same Eaton TVS R2650 blower, now spinning a bit faster, thanks to a smaller-diameter pulley on its nose. This produces a peak of 13.7 psi of boost—up from 12.0 in the GT500—which is enough to bump horsepower to 795 and torque to 660 pound-feet of torque in comparison to 760 horses and 625 pound-feet in the older Shelby GT500. That output drives the rear wheels through the same slick-shifting Tremec seven-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission.
This V-8 also sounds terrific. The active mufflers provide four levels of sound—with Quiet, Normal, Sport, and Track modes—and none of them could be described as shy. The V-8’s cylinder eruptions burst forth even in Quiet mode if you toe into the throttle even a little bit. In Track mode, the car bellows like a NASCAR stocker. When driven in anger, you can hear these cars a block away.
We haven’t yet had the opportunity to properly test the Dark Horse SC, but we did a few runs on the drag strip at Sonoma Raceway. Elapsed times varied from the low 11s to high 10s, with trap speeds in the low to mid-130s. During testing, our best time for the GT500 was 11.3 seconds at 132 mph, and with 35 more ponies, similar weight, and stickier Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R tires (with the Track Pack); we would expect an ET in the high 10s and a few more mph at the trap.
What’s interesting is that despite this exuberant soundtrack and the car’s heroic performance, the Dark Horse SC is remarkably refined. We drove both the standard version (base price: $108,085, including $2600 gas guzzler tax) and one with the Track Pack ($144,585), and both worked great on the street. There’s also a Special Edition model that goes for a lofty $175,565.
It helps that all SCs are equipped with adaptive magnetorheological dampers, which the Ford engineers calibrated superbly. The suspension on both versions we piloted controls body motions tightly while also riding well. The cars also have sharp steering and easily modulated—and giant—brakes.
The Track Pack car is particularly impressive. Despite a slightly stiffer suspension, half-inch wider wheels, and the Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2R tires, the car never banged or crashed on even sharp bumps. With this package, the steering seems particularly responsive and immediate, yet the car is not at all darty on undulating pavement. And the carbon-ceramic brakes that come with the package are even easier to modulate than the base car’s iron stoppers.
The carbon-fiber wheels and carbon-ceramic brakes that come with this package—as well as the deleted rear seats—are said to cut some 150 pounds, with about 120 pounds of that being rotating mass. Maybe there is something to this reducing unsprung weight business.
As part of the test drive, we also got a few hot laps around the Sonoma road course, which, of course, is the current name for the famous Sears Point track, with its infamous carousel and esses.
We were in the Track Pack cars, which have an adjustable rear wing and customer-installed wicker-like appendages on the front splitter. The cars also had the rain tray removed from the hood vents, which increases front downforce substantially.
Total negative lift amounts to 620 pounds at 180 mph—a speed we could never approach on the track. However, the downforce is greater in the rear than the front, which makes for a bit of increasing high-speed understeer—never a bad thing in a fast, challenging corner.
There are six levels of traction control that you can easily adjust when in Track mode, and that provides comforting reassurance when you start pushing this powerful and heavy car. The giant 16.5-inch-diameter and 1.6-inch-thick carbon-ceramic front rotors (the non-Track Pack cars utilize the same size rotors, just constructed from the aforementioned iron) are very powerful and easily slow the car, though in the track environment, they feel touchier than they did on the street. Perhaps higher pad temperatures compromise the initial softness that feels so comfortable at a slower pace.
We never quite got up to full speed in our few laps, but the SC felt fast and responsive. In Track mode, the transmission shifts very well when left to its own devices. It promises to be a great track-day toy. Just don’t use up those carbon-ceramic brakes too quickly. They likely cost 20 big ones to replace.
Taking a long trip in the SC should be reasonably comfortable, with very nice seats, an excellent driving position, and enough luggage space for the clothes you’re likely to need at a Mustang gathering. Despite the great steering, the car’s 76.5-inch width does feel bulky on narrow back roads, but that’s a common problem these days.
The giant screen presents a nice variety of useful instrument display choices and offers the various electronic navigation and entertainment aids we all expect these days. But it feels vaguely out of place in a Mustang, especially as it eliminated the traditional twin-cowl dashboard layout. The HVAC controls are on the screen, but at least they’re decently sized and always visible.
The satisfying, but incessant, exhaust soundtrack might get tedious on a long drive. Other Mustangs might be better choices for such trips. The Dark Horse SC was created for all manner of motorized enjoyment—but long hours in the saddle might not be one of them.

source_texts.title: 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC First-Drive Review: The Perfect Mustang Doesn’t Need a Stick
source_texts.summary: The post 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC First-Drive Review: The Perfect Mustang Doesn’t Need a Stick appeared first on The Drive .
source_texts.text:
The evolution of the supercharged halo-spec Mustang has produced a wild spectrum of machines. Whether it’s Eleanor or something a bit less elegant, the formula has undeniably shaped the automotive landscape. And now there’s a new twist: the 2026 Ford Mustang Dark Horse SC throws out old naming conventions, but the formula remains intact.
Despite the name change, you can draw a straight line between the now-departed Cobra and the new Dark Horse SC. The underlying S650 Mustang chassis is an evolution of the S550, which originally hit the market as a 2015 model. That generation gave us a Bullitt, Mach 1, GT350, and, of course, the 760-horsepower GT500.
Dark Horse SC picks up where GT500 left off. The supercharged, 5.2-liter V8 returns with 795 hp and 660 pound-feet of torque. That power still reaches the rear wheels through a seven-speed dual-clutch automatic and an electronically controlled Torsen limited-slip rear differential. To keep all of that in check, Ford upped the ante on cooling and braking. Check the Track Pack option, and you’ll get 16.5-inch carbon ceramic brakes up front and 14.6 in the rear. The standard car gets equally enormous rotors and the same piston counts (six up front; four in the rear), but they’re made of old-fashioned iron.
The S650’s redesigned nose gave Ford’s engineers more space to draw in air, helping feed the auxiliary radiator and oil cooler mounted in the outboard cut-outs in the SC’s front bumper. Like the standard Dark Horse, the SC carries over the massive heat-extraction vent in the hood. It’s bigger here than on the naturally aspirated Dark Horse, and you can remove the rain tray underneath if you plan to track it. That vent channels heat out of the engine bay and reduces lift on the hood’s underside.
A Little Help From GTD
In the half-decade since Ford introduced the old GT500, we’ve seen another high-output Mustang variant arrive: GTD. In developing that $325,000 track machine, Ford introduced a new speed-dependent traction control system that it later ported to the Dark Horse SC. If the DCT made the GT500’s performance significantly more accessible relative to previous Shelby models, the SC’s new software leans even further in that direction. The GTD also drove the SC’s carbon brake upgrade.
Ford made plenty of other changes and small adjustments, including an overhauled MagneRide suspension and numerous adjustments to the car’s aerodynamic profile. Inside, Ford put together what it describes as a “function-first” cockpit. The S550 DNA shines through brightly in the cabin; it even smells like my old 2015 Mustang GT. I’m pretty sure I could disassemble this interior blindfolded.
Opt for the Track Package, and in addition to the aforementioned performance upgrades, you get teal brake calipers and interior elements, including the seat belts but, curiously, not the upholstery stitching. You also lose the rear bench seat. Add the lighter wheels and brake components, and this spec comes in 150 pounds lighter—much of that unsprung.
A Magnetic Personality
I’m a big believer in adaptive dampers, but I’ve never quite been sold on how they’re executed in the Mustang. In the S550, the car often felt like it was being led around by the nose—not necessarily an appealing sensation in an already front-heavy car.
The primary job of any well-engineered suspension is keeping your tires in contact with the pavement. To accomplish that, it needs to respond quickly to surface bumps and dips. Unfortunately, if you want a stiff setup to minimize weight transfer on a track, that brief can run counter to the suspension’s secondary mission: not liquefying your organs in the process. That dichotomy is what makes adaptive damper tech so clutch.
Ford’s revised MagneRide comes in two flavors: one for the base car and another specific to the Track Pack. And this time around, both are sublime. My memories of corralling a tram-lining S550 Mach 1 through every rutted intersection in southeast Michigan vanished the instant I found bad pavement in the SC.
The testing ground was Napa Valley—far from the environment I just described, but no stranger to lumpy asphalt. The mountain roads are often smooth as glass at their crowns but littered with whoop-de-dos at their margins, especially in shaded spots where temperatures more often dip below freezing.
I expected the constant, uneven undulations to bully the SC’s front end off-line, but those annoying tugs never came. Attacking a long, 55-mph uphill climb, I started with my palms firmly on the wheel. Halfway up, I found myself confidently throwing the wheel around with just my fingertips.
Grip for Days
The Track Pack ships with Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 Rs. The track-ready rubber didn’t balk at the cold, damp surfaces below the fog layer. The SC feels smaller than it is—a rarer and rarer sensation these days—but not so much that it deceives you into pushing harder than you should. Sure, you might need a good stab of the brake if a stop sign sneaks up on you, but those 305/30R20s up front are reluctant to push unless you’re willing to cross the line into truly anti-social driving behavior; the 315s out back likewise pacify the rear.
That’s a common theme with the SC, as it turns out. Hell, even if you want to use all of its throttle, simply finding space to do so is a challenge. The short straights in the mountains invite maybe a second or two of sustained, wide-open throttle before the next rock face starts coming up at you awfully quickly. But you do it anyway, of course, because of that noise. It’s intoxicating. Hearing each upshift crack off the exposed rock is the sort of thing that might entice you to abandon your objective and double back for another round—unless your destination is Sonoma Raceway.
And remember: Sonoma isn’t just a road course. We split our day at the track into two modules. In the morning, quarter-mile passes with a sportsman tree. In the afternoon, the main event: flying laps on the road course’s long configuration. That’s a lot of track, and this is a lot of car. Time to boogie.
If you ask the internet, Sonoma’s quarter-mile strip is a quicker surface than most. Its location in California’s Bay Area is pretty ideal, climate- and elevation-wise. That goes double if you can run it mid-morning, after the sun has started to warm the pavement but before it encourages heat soak. Coincidentally, that lined up perfectly with my itinerary.
Power to the People
You can launch the car one of two ways. You can simply roll into the box and, y’know, do one, or you can get an assist from the SC’s digital line lock. The latter’s pretty neat, but might rival some Tesla gimmicks for the time needed to set the correct mode via the touchscreen and steering wheel. Speaking of which, these animations don’t need to last so long. Bronco, Tremor, and Raptor suffer from the same vanities. Too much fanfare.
